title: Architect the Solution Architecture (Assets)
overview: This topic is the architect's toolbox of reusable assets: architecture styles (structural and communication), reference architectures (web, mobile, broker, SOA, microservices, cloud, serverless) and the way an architecture is described through views and viewpoints (IEEE 42010, UML, 4+1). The idea is that you rarely start from a blank page; you reuse proven patterns and choose among them by quality attributes. For the exam, expect to pick and justify styles and reference architectures for a scenario and to describe the architecture with the right views.
big_ideas: Architectural assets = reference patterns (idioms, design patterns, architecture styles) + reference architectures, used to produce an architecture and its architectural description.
Similar systems lean mostly on reuse; innovative systems lean more on method and intuition.
Structural styles: client-server, tiered (3-tier/n-tier), peer-to-peer. Network zoning uses DMZ, reverse proxy (hides servers) and forward proxy (hides clients).
**During a network partition, CAP forces a trade-off between strict consistency and availability.** ACID consistency means preserving database rules; it is a different use of the word consistency.
Communication styles: data flow (file or database level), call and return (presentation or application level, SOAP/REST), event-based (point-to-point queue, publish/subscribe).
Reference architectures bundle many patterns for a domain: web, mobile, broker/ESB, SOA layers, microservices (scale cube, discovery, API gateway), cloud, serverless; avoid spaghetti.
Microservices scale cube: X = clone, Y = functional decomposition, Z = data partitioning.
Describe architecture with multiple views: 4+1 (logical, process, development, physical + scenarios) and viewpoints tied to stakeholders and concerns.

sections.title: Architectural assets and the metamodel
sections.summary: Why architects reuse assets, and how reference patterns, reference architectures and architectural description relate.

notes.lead: How you derive an architecture depends on the system:

sub: leans **mainly on reuse** of known solutions
relies **more heavily on method and assets**
**reuse** is a smaller (but still present) input

items: An **architecture uses** → **reference patterns** and **reference architectures**
An **architecture is documented by** → an **architectural description**
notes.foot: These **reusable assets** capture earlier solutions; **check their fit** to the current requirements.

items: **Idioms**
**Design patterns**
**Architecture styles** → the **coarse-grained** ones this topic focuses on
**Analysis patterns** → also listed among them in the lecture's summary

terms.def: Reusable proven solution: idiom, design pattern or architecture style.
Domain-specific architecture that bundles many patterns.
The documented description of the architecture (views and viewpoints).

check.q: Your firm has built five online-banking portals and is asked for a sixth, for a new bank. Separately, it is asked to architect a first-of-its-kind drone-delivery control system. How does your approach differ?

sub: **Earlier solutions**, **reference patterns** and a **banking reference architecture**
Check that they **fit this bank's requirements**
Rely more on **method** and on assets that only **partly apply**

a.foot: The risk differs: **reuse** risks carrying over assumptions that no longer fit; an **innovative design** risks **unproven decisions**.

check.q: A team adopts a published retail e-commerce reference architecture for a B2B procurement system with multi-level approvals. What do they gain, and what must they check?

items: **Gain**: a **proven structure** that bundles many **patterns** → cuts **logical design effort**
**Check fit**: a reference architecture is **tied to its domain** → B2B **approval workflows** and integration with **buyers' systems** may not appear in a retail reference at all
**Adapt**: keep what fits, **add patterns for the gaps**, and **record where you departed** from the reference

center.label: Architecture
center.detail: Reuse patterns and reference architectures where they fit, then document the resulting design with views addressing stakeholder concerns.

items.label: Reference patterns
items.detail: Many per architecture. Capture proven successes of the past.

items.label: Reference architectures
items.detail: Many per architecture. Typically include many architectural patterns.

items.label: Architectural description
items.detail: Collects the views and rationale needed to explain the architecture to its stakeholders.

sections.title: Structural styles and deployment components
sections.summary: Client-server and tiered styles, the network zones and proxies used to deploy them, and the server component types.

items: **Server** offers services through **well-defined interfaces**
**Clients** use them → browser, applet, mobile app
**Several tiers cooperate** → **3-tier, n-tier**
Each tier acts as **server to its caller** and **client to the next**

sub: segregate by **layers, features or organisation structure**

items: **Example in the lecture** → **public web reverse proxy** in a **DMZ**
Separated from **internal application and database servers** by an **inner firewall**
Some **supporting servers** also appear in its DMZ
Placement is **an example, not a rule** for all deployments
**Permit only required traffic** between zones
**Reverse proxy** → sits **in front of internal servers**, serving **internet users**, hides the **servers' identity**
**Forward proxy** → provides **internet access** to **firewall-restricted internal clients**, hides the **clients' identity**
**Service execution** → application servers
**B2C integration** → portal servers
**Service and B2B integration** → API gateway, ESB, BPM suites, B2B gateways
**Management and governance** → MDM, MAM, service registry
**Data persistence** → SQL, NoSQL

terms.def: Network segment separating a purely internal network from an external network.
Server in front of internal servers facing internet users; hides server identity.
Server giving restricted internal clients internet access; hides client identity.
Enterprise Service Bus: service and B2B integration component.
Architecture of several computational tiers, each server to the one above and client to the one below.

check.q: Staff on the internal network need controlled internet access, and internet customers need to reach the company's web servers. Which kind of proxy fits each, and what does each hide?

items: **Staff → forward proxy**: gives firewall-restricted internal clients internet access; **hides the clients'** identity
**Customers → reverse proxy**: typically in the **DMZ**, fronts the internal servers; **hides theirs**
a.foot: Using one for the other's job would **expose the wrong side**.

check.q: A design puts the web server, application server and database all in the DMZ 'to keep latency low'. Critique it.

items: **Problem**: everything is exposed in the **outer zone** → compromising the web server gives direct reach to the application and the data
**DMZ**: keep only the internet-facing **reverse proxy or web tier** there
**Inner firewall**: put the application and database servers behind it
**Permit only** the traffic each needs
a.foot: Cost: an extra **network boundary** and more **firewall rules** to manage → buys a much smaller **blast radius**.

check.q: A field-inspection app must keep working in areas with no mobile signal and sync later. Thick or thin client, and what design questions does that raise?

a.lead: **Thick client**: it needs local logic and storage to work **offline**. That raises the **client-server design questions**:
items: **Logic split**: how to split logic between client and server
**State**: how to manage state and **reconcile** changes made offline
**Security**: how to **authenticate and authorise** without a live connection
a.foot: You give up **easy updates** and accept **more data on devices**, which must be protected.

visuals.title: Typical zoned deployment (internet user to data)

steps.label: Internet clients
steps.detail: Clients reach the public entry point rather than directly accessing internal servers.

steps.label: DMZ proxy
steps.detail: The outer firewall admits required public traffic. The reverse proxy handles requests at the exposed boundary.

steps.label: Application tier
steps.detail: The inner firewall permits only required proxy-to-application traffic, limiting paths into the internal zone.

steps.label: Database tier
steps.detail: The application accesses persistence through explicitly permitted connections; internet clients do not connect directly.

sections.title: SQL vs NoSQL, CAP, ACID vs BASE, peer-to-peer
sections.summary: Data persistence trade-offs a structural style forces: relational vs NoSQL, the CAP theorem, ACID vs BASE, and the peer-to-peer style.

notes.lead: They describe **data models**, not guaranteed scaling or consistency.
items: **Relational (SQL)** → tables and **declared schemas** (MySQL, Postgres, Oracle)
**Scaling** → lecture contrasts typical **vertical SQL** and **horizontal NoSQL** scaling
Actual capabilities **depend on the product and configuration**

notes.h: CAP applies during a network partition
items: **Consistency** → operations behave like **one up-to-date copy**
**Availability** → **every request to a non-failing node** receives a response
**Partition** → if nodes cannot communicate, a distributed store **cannot guarantee both**
notes.foot: This is **not** a general instruction to **pick any two** properties for normal operation.

items: **Atomicity** → all or none
**Consistency** → preserve database rules
**Isolation** → control interference between concurrent transactions
**Durability** → committed changes survive
notes.foot: **ACID consistency differs from CAP consistency.** An ACID label alone does not describe **partition behaviour**.

items: **Basically available**
**Soft state**
**Eventual consistency** → replicas may **temporarily disagree** and **converge later**
notes.foot: Describes an **approach to distributed state**, not a promise that every NoSQL store lacks transactions or durability.

items: **Persist carts**
**Browsing and cart updates** → may **tolerate stale data** to remain **available**
**Checkout and payment** → need **coordinated, correct updates**; may **wait or reject** requests during a partition
notes.foot: State the **acceptable staleness** and **failure behaviour** rather than choosing solely by database label.

items: Peers act as **both clients and servers** and **communicate directly**
**Lecture examples** → Napster, BitTorrent, games, Bitcoin
May still use **supporting discovery services**
**Consider** → consistency, authentication and authorisation

terms.def: During a network partition, a distributed shared-data system cannot guarantee both strict consistency and availability.
Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.
Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency.
Peers can each act as client and server and communicate directly; supporting coordination may still exist.

check.q: A ride-hailing platform runs in two data centres. During a network partition between them, which operations would you let answer with possibly stale data, and which would you make wait or reject: showing nearby drivers, updating a profile photo, charging the rider's card?

items: **Nearby drivers, profile photos → favour availability**: slightly stale data is acceptable and reconciles later
**Charging the card → favour consistency**: wait or fail rather than risk a **double or lost charge**
a.foot: **CAP is applied per operation** during a partition → state the **acceptable staleness** for each one rather than choosing by database label.

check.q: A teammate says: 'Our database is ACID, so it stays consistent even when the two regions lose contact.' Do you agree?

items: **ACID consistency**: a transaction preserves the **database's rules**
**CAP consistency**: all nodes behave like **one up-to-date copy** during a **partition**
An **ACID label** says nothing about what the system does when regions cannot communicate
a.foot: Check the product's **replication and partition behaviour**, and decide **per operation** whether to reject requests or serve stale data.

check.q: A team picks a NoSQL document store for an invoicing system 'because NoSQL scales horizontally and SQL doesn't'. Invoices need atomic updates across customer, invoice and ledger records. Critique the choice.

a.lead: The reasoning uses a **label, not the requirement**.
items: **Tendencies, not guarantees**: the lecture presents **horizontal NoSQL** and **vertical SQL** scaling as tendencies
**Deciding need**: coordinated **multi-record updates** → a relational **ACID** store supports them directly
**Check**: the expected volume and each product's actual **transaction and scaling options**
a.foot: If volume were **huge** and the data naturally **document-shaped**, the balance could change.

check.q: A company must push 2 GB software updates to 20,000 branch PCs over thin WAN links. Would a peer-to-peer style fit, and what concerns would you raise?

a.lead: **It can fit**: peers act as both clients and servers, so branches share pieces locally instead of all downloading from the centre (the **BitTorrent** pattern). Concerns to raise:
items: **Authenticating and authorising peers**
**Consistency**: keeping updates consistent and **untampered** across peers
**Discovery service**: peers still rely on it
a.foot: If the links could handle a central download, a simpler **client-server** distribution avoids those problems.

visuals.title: What happens during a partition?
rows: Prevent conflicting checkout or payment updates
Allow temporarily stale catalogue or cart data

sections.title: Communication styles and integration levels
sections.summary: The three communication styles (data flow, call and return, event-based), the integration level at which each is used and the technologies behind them.

items: Data **enters and passes through components one at a time** to a final destination
Suits **batch integration (ETL)**
**Concerns** → error handling, acceptable processing time, one- vs two-way replication

sub: legacy integration with few technology options

items: Component **runs when it receives control** and **returns control when done** (OSI layers, OS layers)
**Concerns** → discovering the target, error handling, timeouts

sub: extending legacy systems to the web without source code
integrating existing systems in a process

items: **Queue** routes **each message to one consumer** for processing
**Producer need not wait** for the business operation to finish
notes.foot: **Asynchrony does not by itself guarantee delivery.**

items: **Subscribers register interest**; publisher sends to **any number** of them
**Examples** → forum subscriptions, push notifications
**Concerns** → asynchrony, durable vs non-durable, single point of failure

notes.lead: Match it to the **required qualities** and **coupling**.
items: **Synchronous call and return** → simple, but **couples caller and callee in time**
**Event-based** → **decouples** and **handles load**, but **adds complexity**
**Public needs** → availability, performance, usability for **rich graphics**
**Data already sits** in a **sensor system**
**So** → **database-level data flow** or **web-service call and return** can feed a **web front end**

terms.def: Extract-Transform-Load: typical data flow batch integration.
Integrating several databases through a single virtual view.
Presentation-level integration by reading a legacy system's user interface.
Web service styles for application-level call and return.
Publisher announces events to any number of registered subscribers.

check.q: An order service must (a) hand each payment job to exactly one of several payment workers and (b) tell inventory, email and analytics that an order was placed. Which messaging style suits each?

items: **(a) Point-to-point queue**: each message goes to **one consumer** → workers share the jobs
**(b) Publish/subscribe**: each subscriber gets the event → new subscribers can be added **without changing the order service**
a.foot: In both, delivery depends on **configuration**: use **persistent messages**, **acknowledgements** and **durable subscriptions** if consumers can be offline.

check.q: Management wants a near-real-time sales dashboard combining three regional databases. An engineer proposes nightly FTP exports. Do you agree?

items: **File-level data flow** suits large **scheduled batches** and **legacy systems** with few options
**Real-time reporting and dashboards** = a **database-level** use case (**views, federation or replication**)
**Trade-off**: database-level integration **couples you to the source schemas** and needs **database access**
a.foot: If the regions can **only export files**, you are forced to file level and must accept **stale data**.

check.q: A 25-year-old application has no API, its source code is lost, and the business wants its data on a new web portal next quarter. What integration do you choose, and what are the risks?

a.lead: **Presentation-level integration (screen scraping)** is the realistic choice: it suits extending a legacy system to the web without source code.
items: **Fragile**: any screen change breaks it
**Slow**
**Limited** to what the screens show
a.foot: If its database turns out to be accessible, **database-level data flow** would be more robust.

check.q: Checkout calls fraud check, inventory, loyalty points and email synchronously, one after another. The loyalty service is often slow, and checkout times out. What would you change?

items: **Keep call-and-return**: fraud check and inventory → the checkout result depends on them
**Move to event-based messaging**: loyalty and email → a slow service no longer holds checkout
**Why**: synchronous calls **couple the caller to the callee in time**, while events **decouple** them
a.foot: Cost: extra **complexity** and loyalty points that update a little later → add **retries and failure handling** for the asynchronous path.

visuals.title: Communication styles and where they integrate

items.label: Data flow
items.detail: File level: FTP for large scheduled batches and legacy. Database level: views, federation, replication for single customer view and dashboards.

items.label: Call and return
items.detail: Presentation level: URL access, screen scraping. Application level: RPC, SOAP/REST web services for B2B.

items.label: Event: point-to-point
items.detail: A queue distributes work among consumers. Define acknowledgement, persistence, retries and ordering rather than assuming messages are processed exactly once.

items.label: Event: publish/subscribe
items.detail: Each relevant subscription can receive the event. Durable versus non-durable subscriptions determine what happens while a subscriber is absent.

sections.title: Reference architectures: web and mobile
sections.summary: What a reference architecture is, the web architecture and its AWS mapping, and the shift to client-centric mobile architecture.

items: Belongs to a **domain** and **bundles many patterns**
**Deck covers** → web, mobile, broker, SOA and microservices, cloud and serverless
**Anti-example** → **spaghetti 'architecture'**: components tangled with no structure

notes.lead: Each concern maps to a service:
items: **DNS routing** → Route 53
**Content delivery** at the **nearest edge location** for low latency → CloudFront
**Static content storage** → S3
**Load balancing** across instances
**Web and application servers** → dynamic content
**Auto scaling** → adjust capacity up or down
**Multi-AZ managed database**
**Persistent session store** → the cart
**Volatile session store and cache** → the catalogue
**Search**
**Secure SSL checkout**
**Log-based recommendations**
Moves **rendering** and **some application logic** to a **browser or native app** that calls **backend APIs**
**Server-side services still** enforce **business rules** and **protect data**
notes.foot: The shift concerns **where presentation and interaction run**.

items: Choices driven by **decision drivers** the deck leaves open (e.g. **native vs hybrid vs web**)
**IBM and AWS** both publish mobile reference architectures
Combine **device app**, **API/backend services** and **enterprise integration**

terms.def: Domain-level architecture combining many patterns as a reusable template.
App runs on the client and consumes APIs and services rather than receiving server-rendered pages.
Content delivery point close to users for low latency.

check.q: A news site's application servers run at 90% CPU, mostly serving images and scripts, and readers abroad see slow page loads. What would you change, following the web reference architecture?

a.lead: Move **static content** to **object storage** and serve it through a **content delivery network**.
items: **Offload**: takes static load off the application servers → left for **dynamic content**
**Latency**: serves readers from the nearest **edge location**
a.foot: It does not speed up **slow dynamic pages**, and **updated content** must reach the edge copies.

check.q: An e-commerce site keeps shopping carts in web-server memory. During a scale-in event, customers lose their carts. Diagnose and fix.

items: **Diagnosis**: the cart state lives in the **instance that was removed**
**Fix**, as in the **e-commerce reference**: put carts in a **persistent session store** that survives instance loss
**Fast in-memory store**: for volatile session data and **catalogue caching**
a.foot: Cost: another component to run and a **network hop** per cart access → in return **any instance can serve any customer**.

check.q: A bank moves from server-rendered pages to a single-page app calling APIs. A developer proposes moving the transfer-limit check into the browser to save a round trip. Do you agree?

items: **Client-centric architecture**: rendering and interaction move to the client
**Server-side services** must still **enforce business rules** and protect data → client code **can be bypassed**
a.foot: A browser-side check is fine for **quick feedback**, as long as the **server repeats it**.

sections.title: Broker, SOA and microservices
sections.summary: Broker/ESB event channels, the five-layer SOA reference architecture and the microservices style with its scale cube, discovery and API gateway.

items: **Events** go into **event channels**, handled by **independent event processors** (modules)
**Examples (ESBs)** → WebSphere ESB, Apache Camel, Mule
**Process orchestration** sits on top (e.g. **BizTalk**)
**Consumer** → portal
**Integration** and **Business Process**
**Services**
**Component**
**Operational Systems** → runtime, legacy and packaged back ends
**Portal** on top
**Process orchestration** beneath
**Services** supporting the process
**Components** implementing services
**Systems** running them
Split the system into **vertical slices** instead of **horizontal layers**
Each **owns its own data store**
**Cost** → **hundreds of services** form a **dense web of dependencies**
So the style **demands** → **service discovery**, **gateways** and **automation**
**X axis** → **horizontal duplication** (scale by **cloning**)
**Y axis** → **functional decomposition** (scale by **splitting different things**, i.e. **microservices**)
**Z axis** → **data partitioning** (scale by **splitting similar things**, i.e. **sharding**)

sub: clients call a **router** at a **well-known location**

items: **API gateway** → the **single entry point** that **routes, aggregates** and **shields clients** from the service layout

terms.def: Broker pathway through which events flow to event processors.
Directory of live service instances queried during discovery.
Single entry point for clients that routes to microservices.
X cloning, Y functional decomposition, Z data partitioning.
A service aligned to a business capability, owning its logic and data rather than sharing horizontal technical layers.

check.q: A retail system's search service is overloaded at peak, its order table has grown to 2 billion rows, and the promotions and payments teams keep blocking each other's releases. Which scale-cube axis addresses each problem?

items: **Search load → X axis**: clone more **identical instances** behind a **load balancer**
**Huge order table → Z axis**: **partition data** (for example by customer) so each instance handles a subset
**Team collisions → Y axis**: split **by function** into separate services

check.q: A team lists service instance addresses in configuration files. After auto-scaling is switched on, calls fail intermittently. Diagnose and fix.

items: **Diagnosis**: instances are now **ephemeral** → new ones are missing from the files and removed ones are still being called
**Fix: service discovery** → clients call a **router** at a **well-known location**, which looks up available instances in a **service registry**
a.foot: The registry then becomes **critical infrastructure** and needs its own **high availability**.

check.q: All 40 integrations in a bank flow through one ESB instance, and an ESB upgrade took every channel offline for an evening. What risk did this expose, and what would you consider?

a.lead: The **broker style's main risk**: the central broker is a **single point of failure** and a potential **bottleneck**.
items: Make the broker **redundant** and **upgradable without an outage**
Move integrations that need **no central orchestration** to **direct or event-based links**
a.foot: You give up some **central governance** in exchange for **resilience**.

check.q: A 10-person team with one product and weekly releases is told to split its layered monolith into 30 microservices. Do you agree?

items: **Microservices give**: independently deployable, scalable **vertical slices**
**Cost**: a dense **web of dependencies**; needs **service discovery**, **gateways** and **automation**
**One team**, manageable release pace → operational cost likely **outweighs the benefit**
a.foot: **Modularise the monolith** first; split out a service when a part needs **independent scaling** or **more teams** join.

sections.title: Cloud, serverless and reactive
sections.summary: Cloud reference architecture, service and deployment models, VMs vs containers, multitenancy and elasticity, serverless, and the Reactive Manifesto.

items: **Wrapped by** → governance and security, resiliency, performance, consumability
**Three roles** → service **creator**, **consumer**, **provider**
**Provider's common cloud management platform** → supplies **operational and business support services**
Over **cloud services** at **IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and BPaaS** levels
**Private** → on-site or outsourced
**Community** → on-site or outsourced
**Public**
**Hybrid**
**VM** → each includes a **guest OS**
**Container** → **shares a host kernel**, packages the **app with its dependencies**
A **hosted hypervisor** is one arrangement
notes.foot: The key distinction is the **guest OS boundary** versus a **shared kernel**.

items: **Multitenancy** → **isolation** of independent organisations' **workloads** in a **shared environment**
**Elasticity** → provisioning resources **in proportion to changing demand**, up or down
e.g. **Lambda**
You **supply functions**; the platform **runs and scales** them
You **do not manage servers**
**Complements microservices**
**Responsive** → consistent response times with **reliable upper bounds**
**Elastic** → stay responsive under **varying workload**
**Resilient** → stay responsive in the **face of failure**
**Asynchronous message passing** → gives **loose coupling**, **isolation** and **location transparency**

terms.def: Isolating independent organisations' workloads in a shared environment.
Provisioning resources in proportion to changing needs, up or down.
Lightweight packaged app sharing the host OS kernel via a container engine.
Combination of private and public cloud (NIST deployment model).
Responsive, resilient, elastic and message-driven system.

check.q: You must run 200 small instances of the same Linux service, and also host a legacy application that needs its own OS kernel version. Containers or VMs for each?

items: **200 instances → containers**: share the **host kernel** and package only the application and its dependencies → **lighter and denser**
**Legacy application → VM**: it needs its own **guest OS**
a.foot: The trade-off is **isolation**: a VM has a **guest OS boundary**, while containers **share one kernel**.

check.q: A SaaS payroll provider hosts 300 client companies on shared infrastructure, and load spikes at each month end. Which cloud property addresses which concern?

items: **Multitenancy → sharing**: each company's workloads and data must stay **isolated** in the common environment
**Elasticity → the spike**: resources are **provisioned up** for month end and **back down** afterwards
a.foot: They interact: elastic capacity without good **tenant isolation** lets one tenant's spike **degrade the others**.

check.q: An image-thumbnail job runs a few hundred times a day, with occasional bursts of several thousand. Serverless functions or always-on containers?

items: **You supply the function**; the platform runs and scales it
**No servers** to manage
**No paying for idle capacity** between bursts
a.foot: You give up **control over the runtime environment**. If the load became **steady and high**, re-examine whether **always-on instances** are better value.

check.q: A service blocks one thread per request while calling a slow partner API. Under peak load it stops responding entirely. What would the Reactive Manifesto suggest?

a.lead: Use **asynchronous message passing**, so a slow partner does not tie up a **thread per request**.
items: **Loose coupling and isolation**
**Elastic**: keeps the service responsive under varying load
**Resilient**: responsive when the partner fails
a.foot: Cost: a more complex **programming and failure-handling model**.

sections.title: Architectural description: views and viewpoints
sections.summary: How architecture is documented: IEEE 42010 metamodel, UML, the 4+1 view model and further viewpoints aimed at specific stakeholders.

notes.lead: Standard for **architecture description** (building on **IEEE 1471**). Key idea:
items: **Stakeholders** have **concerns**
A **viewpoint** addresses those concerns with **modelling techniques**
A **view** is the viewpoint **applied to the system**
**General-purpose standard notation**
**Structure** and **behaviour** diagram types
**Examples** → class, component, package, deployment, sequence, activity, state

notes.lead: Several **concurrent views** tied to scenarios (view → stakeholder: concerns):
items: **Logical** → end user: functionality
**Process** → integrator: performance, security, throughput
**Development** → programmer: coding, testing
**Physical** → system engineer: topology, delivery, installation, telecommunication
**+1 Scenarios** → tie the four together

notes.lead: Each has **stakeholders, concerns and techniques** (viewpoint → techniques):
items: **Organization** → block diagram
**Business Function** → block diagram
**Business Process** → block, BPMN, BPEL, UML activity
**Application Structure** → layering, UML package, component
**Application Behaviour** → sequence, collaboration, state
**Infrastructure** → network, package, block (concerns: security, stability, cost)
**Deployment** → UML package, deployment diagrams (mapping **logical components to physical artifacts**)
**Information Structure** → UML class, ER
**Metamodel** → reference patterns, reference architectures, architectural description
**Reference patterns include** → architecture styles, analysis patterns, design patterns, idioms
**Choosing the right style and architecture** depends on the **architect's knowledge and experience**
notes.foot: The right choice is **critical to achieving the required qualities**.

terms.def: Conventions for a kind of view: which stakeholders, concerns and modelling techniques.
Representation of the system from one viewpoint.
Logical, process, development and physical views tied by scenarios.
Unified Modeling Language, standard visual notation for software design.
Business Process Model and Notation, used for business process viewpoints.

check.q: An architect presents one large diagram mixing classes, servers, network zones and business process steps. Operations staff and developers both say it doesn't answer their questions. What would you change?

a.lead: Split it into **views** aimed at each **stakeholder's concerns**, as **ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010** suggests:
items: **Physical or deployment view** → operations
**Development view** → programmers
**Logical view** → functionality
**Process view** → performance
**Key scenarios** → tie them together
a.foot: Cost: keeping several views **consistent**, which the scenarios help with.

check.q: Three concerns are raised: an integrator asks about throughput between concurrent processes; a system engineer asks how components are installed across sites; programmers ask how code modules are organised for testing. Which 4+1 view answers each?

items: **Integrator → process view**: performance, throughput, concurrency
**System engineer → physical view**: topology, installation, delivery
**Programmers → development view**: code organisation, testing
**Scenarios**: check that the three views describe the **same system**

check.q: A team defines a deployment viewpoint but supplies no deployment view. What is missing?
check.a: The viewpoint sets the conventions and concerns; the view applies them to this system. The team still needs the actual mapping of components and artifacts to nodes, with the relevant connections.

check.q: A security auditor asks which components run in the DMZ and which can talk to the database. Which viewpoint and notation would you use?

items: **Deployment viewpoint**: **UML deployment diagrams** → map logical components to **physical nodes**
**Infrastructure viewpoint**: a **network diagram** → **zones** and **permitted connections**
a.foot: A **logical component diagram** alone cannot answer it, because it doesn't say **where anything runs**.

center.label: Scenarios
center.detail: Use cases that tie the four views together and validate them.

items.label: Logical view
items.detail: Functionality the system provides to users.

items.label: Process view
items.detail: Performance, security and throughput: runtime behaviour.

items.label: Development view
items.detail: Coding and testing: how the software is organised for development.

items.label: Physical view
items.detail: System topology, delivery, installation and telecommunication.

exam_angles.q: A retailer's legacy inventory system offers only a nightly CSV export and read access to its database. A new web shop needs stock levels no more than 1 minute old, synchronous order placement, and order notifications to email, SMS and analytics. (a) Choose a communication style and integration level for each need. (b) The inventory team then forbids direct database access. What changes?

sub: **Stock → database-level data flow** (replication or a view): **1-minute freshness** rules out the nightly file
**Orders → application-level call and return** through a **web service**: the customer needs an **immediate result**
**Notifications → publish/subscribe**: email, SMS and analytics subscribe independently; new channels need **no change to the order service**
**Structurally**: a **tiered client-server** design with a **reverse proxy in the DMZ**

items.t: **(b) No database access** → only the **file export** remains
sub: Either **negotiate an application-level interface** on the inventory system
Or **accept stale stock data** and show availability as **approximate**
Document this as a **constraint-driven decision** with its **business impact**

exam_angles.q: A concert-ticketing platform runs in two regions. During an on-sale for 20,000 seats, the regions lose contact for 2 minutes. Which operations favour availability and which favour consistency? What does the customer see, and does an ACID database settle the question?

items: **Favour availability**: browsing events and **seat maps** → accept briefly stale seat maps
**Favour consistency**: **seat reservation and payment** → otherwise two regions could sell the same seat
**During the partition**: those operations **wait or are refused** in the region that cannot coordinate → the customer sees a **'try again' or queue message**
**When the link returns**: **reconcile holds**
**ACID doesn't settle it**: ACID transactions guarantee rules **within a transaction** but say nothing about **partition behaviour** → check the **replication design** separately

exam_angles.q: A five-year-old monolith: during sales the catalogue gets 50 times the traffic of checkout; three teams work on it; a nightly report reads every table. Propose a decomposition using the scale cube and name two side effects to monitor.

items: **Y axis**: split by **business capability** (catalogue, checkout, accounts), each service **owning its data** → teams deploy independently
**X axis**: **clone the catalogue** service heavily for sales peaks without scaling checkout
**Z axis**: **partition order data** later if it grows too large
**Add** an **API gateway** and **service discovery**
**Nightly report**: can no longer read every table → feed it from **events or replicas**

sub: **Cross-service consistency** (orders referring to changed catalogue data)
**Latency and failures** across the new **network call chains** → need **tracing and timeouts**

exam_angles.q: Compare two organisations. A bank has 15 legacy core systems, and loan approval is a long process orchestrated across six of them. A start-up has one product, two teams and frequent releases. Would you lean towards broker/SOA or microservices for each, and why?

sub: **Process orchestration** in the **integration layer**, reusing **enterprise services**
Make the **broker redundant**: it is a **single point of failure** and a **bottleneck** risk
Independent **vertical slices** with their **own data** favour **agility**
But only once the team can support **discovery, gateways and automation**

a.foot: **Deciding factors**: the number of systems to integrate, the complexity of **orchestration** and the team's **operational maturity**.

exam_angles.q: A new payments platform is reviewed by an auditor (where card data flows and who can reach it), operations (servers, sites, failover) and developers (module structure, build). How would you document the architecture, and how do you keep the views consistent?

a.lead: Follow **42010**: list the **stakeholders** and their **concerns**, then choose **viewpoints**.
items: **Auditor**: an **information-structure view** (class or ER model) for card data, plus **deployment and infrastructure views** showing **zones and permitted connections**
**Operations**: the **physical or deployment view**, with nodes, sites and **failover paths**
**Developers**: the **development view** and an **application-structure view** (packages, components)
**Process view**: for throughput and concurrency
**Consistency**: tie the views together with **key scenarios** such as 'authorise a card payment', and **trace each scenario through every view**

exam_angles.q: An exam-results portal is idle most of the year, then 200,000 students log in during the first hour of results day. The results are personal data under strict regulation. Which reference-architecture options would you weigh, and what do you give up with each?

a.lead: The demand profile calls for **elasticity**: capacity that scales up for one hour and back down.

sub: Or **serverless functions** for the **read-heavy results lookup**, which scale without managed servers

items.t: **Private or hybrid deployment**: data sensitivity pushes the other way
sub: Keep the **results store** in a **controlled environment**
Put only the **elastic front end** in public cloud
**Give up**: private hosting gives up **elasticity**, forcing you to **provision for the peak**

a.foot: Judge the options by **availability** on results day, **security**, **cost** and **responsiveness** under the spike, the **Reactive** goal.
